content: Programs aimed at improving retention in HIV care should provide community support for individuals living with HIV. This recommendation is strongly supported, although the evidence quality is low. Community-level interventions that have shown benefits in enhancing retention include: 1. Community-based intervention packages: These involve patient advocates, treatment support, and peer support interventions that provide adherence and psychosocial support within the community. Evidence quality is low for children and very low for adults. 2. Adherence clubs: These clubs offer peer support, distribution of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, and assessments by non-clinical or lay providers. Evidence quality is moderate. 3. Extra care for high-risk individuals: This includes additional support for those at higher risk of poor outcomes. Evidence quality is very low. Retention in HIV care is critical for achieving sustained viral suppression and improving patient outcomes. However, retention rates vary widely, with some countries reporting rates as low as 60% after three years on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Factors contributing to loss to follow-up include distance to healthcare facilities, lack of transportation, stigma, disclosure-related issues, severe illness, and a lack of understanding of the need for lifelong care. Community-based interventions have demonstrated positive impacts on retention. These include patient-centered support, counseling, and psychosocial support provided by lay adherence counselors or patient advocates. These individuals link health facilities with communities, provide counseling, and visit patients in their homes. For example, one study involving children and adolescents showed significantly improved retention at 36 months, despite the overall low quality of evidence. Adherence clubs have also been effective in reducing loss to follow-up and mortality. These clubs involve brief assessments by non-clinical health workers, referrals to nurses when necessary, peer support, and ART distribution every two months. Long-term follow-up and mortality rates were significantly reduced at 40 months, although the evidence quality remains very low. The cost of implementing community-level interventions varies depending on the setting and whether community-based health programs are already established. Generally, the costs of training and remunerating lay providers are lower than facility-based care costs. Community support, peer support, and patient advocate programs often require investments in training and orientation. Equity and acceptability of interventions are also important considerations. Lay health workers, particularly those living with HIV, family and friend support, mobile health (mHealth) interventions, and non-judgmental relationships with intervention implementers have been identified as acceptable strategies for improving retention. Specific populations face unique challenges in retention and adherence: Pregnant and breastfeeding women: The transition from antenatal care to ART care is a critical point for loss to follow-up. Interventions such as phone calls, SMS reminders, and structured counseling sessions have shown moderate-quality evidence for improving retention in the early postpartum period. However, data on long-term impacts and cost-effectiveness are limited. Children: Caregivers play a crucial role in ensuring children remain in care. Disclosure to children often occurs late, complicating discussions about the importance of follow-up. Age-appropriate disclosure and caregiver support are essential. Adolescents: Frequent clinic visits, long waiting times, and school disruptions discourage engagement in care. Negative attitudes from health workers, privacy concerns, and financial barriers further hinder retention. Peer-based interventions and community-based services are highly valued by adolescents. Flexible appointment systems, comprehensive services addressing psychosocial and sexual health needs, and proactive follow-up strategies are recommended. Men: Men are at a higher risk of death on ART compared to women, partly due to late diagnosis and delayed ART initiation. Innovative service delivery models are needed to improve men’s access to HIV care. Routine disaggregation of data by sex is essential for monitoring treatment outcomes. People with mental health conditions and substance use: Uncontrolled depressive symptoms and substance use are associated with poor ART adherence. Counseling for HIV and depression, along with appropriate medical therapies, can improve adherence. Alcohol and substance use contribute to forgetfulness, poor organization, and diversion of resources, further complicating adherence. Implementation of community and peer support interventions must be adapted to local contexts. Some patients may avoid community-based services due to stigma and discrimination. Effective linkage between community interventions and health facilities is necessary for smooth patient transfer and referral. Strategic planning and resource allocation are critical for sustainability. Community-level programs should be integrated into national health sector plans. Research gaps remain in evaluating different models of community-level support across various contexts. Innovative approaches and effective strategies are needed to support transitions across care delivery points for men, postpartum women, adolescents, and children. Further data on the costs of implementing community-level interventions will guide national policy development.
